note.simple: Two carbons sharing one pair of electrons. The ends can spin around this bond.
note.deeper: A sigma bond, about 1.54 angstroms long. Free rotation about it lets saturated chains coil and tangle.

note.simple: Two carbons sharing two pairs of electrons. It holds the molecule flat and stops it twisting.
note.deeper: A sigma bond plus a pi bond, about 1.33 angstroms, shorter than the 1.54 angstrom single bond in ethane. The pi bond can open up so monomers link into a chain: that is how polyethylene, polystyrene and the rubber in ABS are made.

note.simple: Six carbons in a flat hexagon. The electrons are shared all the way around the ring, which makes it very stable.
note.deeper: An aromatic ring: six pi electrons spread evenly over the ring, so every C-C bond is the same length (1.40 angstroms), between a double bond and a single bond. Drawn here with alternating single and double bonds (a Kekule structure).

note.simple: This end is the 'acid' in lactic acid. It can join to the OH end of another lactic acid.
note.deeper: A carboxylic acid. When it reacts with an alcohol (OH) the two lose a water molecule and form an ester link: that is how lactic acid units join into PLA.

note.simple: The other joining point. An OH on one lactic acid meets the acid end of the next.
note.deeper: A secondary alcohol on the chiral carbon. Lactic acid is a hydroxy acid: it carries both halves of an ester on the same small molecule.

note.simple: This carbon holds four different things, so lactic acid comes in a left-handed and a right-handed form, like gloves. Bacteria can make almost pure left-handed (L) lactic acid.
note.deeper: The stereocentre is (S) in L-lactic acid. Microbial fermentation can give up to 99.9% L; the ratio of L to D units in PLA largely controls how much of it can crystallise.

name: L-lactide (two lactic acids in a ring)

note.simple: Two lactic acids joined head to tail, twice, so they close into a ring. Factories pop this ring open to grow long PLA chains.
note.deeper: A cyclic diester (a dilactone). Ring-opening polymerisation of lactide, usually with a tin catalyst, is the most common route to high molecular weight PLA.

note.simple: A stiff, flat ring in the middle. It is what makes PET and PETG rigid.
note.deeper: A para-disubstituted benzene ring: the two acid groups point in opposite directions, so the chain runs straight through the ring.

note.simple: One of two joining points, one at each end.
note.deeper: A carboxylic acid; it forms an ester with a diol such as ethylene glycol or CHDM.

note.simple: A joining point. Ethylene glycol has one at each end, so it can link two acids.
note.deeper: A primary alcohol. A diol (two OH groups) plus a diacid gives a polyester.

note.simple: A big puckered ring of six carbons. Swapped in for some of the small ethylene glycol, it stops the chains lining up neatly.
note.deeper: 1,4-cyclohexanedimethanol has six more carbons than the ethylene glycol it replaces, so it does not fit the PET crystal: crystallisation is disrupted and the melting point drops. That glycol modification is the G in PETG.

note.simple: One of two joining points.
note.deeper: A primary alcohol; CHDM is a diol, like ethylene glycol.

note.simple: A very eager joining point. It grabs the OH end of a diol and makes a urethane link.
note.deeper: Isocyanates react with alcohols by addition (no water given off) to form carbamates, called urethanes. MDI has two, so it can link two diols.

note.simple: One of two stiff rings that make the hard part of TPU hard.
note.deeper: Aromatic diisocyanates such as MDI are cheap and reactive; polyurethanes made from them tend to darken in sunlight.

note.simple: A joining point at each end. Butanediol is short, so it links MDI molecules into tight, stiff hard segments.
note.deeper: In TPU it is the chain extender: a short diol that reacts with diisocyanate to build the hard segments.

note.simple: This double bond opens up so the molecule can join a chain.
note.deeper: A vinyl group; it polymerises by chain growth (free radical) with styrene.

note.simple: A carbon and a nitrogen joined by three bonds. Nitriles on neighbouring chains pull on each other, which makes the plastic stiffer and tougher.
note.deeper: The C-N triple bond is strongly polar; dipole attraction between nitrile groups binds SAN chains together and raises heat and chemical resistance.

note.simple: Butadiene has two double bonds. When it joins a chain one of them opens up, and the other one stays in the chain.
note.deeper: A conjugated diene. 1,4 addition leaves one C=C in every repeat unit of polybutadiene, which keeps the rubber soft but leaves it open to attack by oxygen, ozone and sunlight.

note.simple: This double bond opens up so the molecule can join a chain.
note.deeper: A vinyl group; it polymerises by chain growth with acrylonitrile to make SAN.

note.simple: A bulky flat ring hanging off the chain. It makes the plastic hard and glassy.
note.deeper: The phenyl side group adds hardness and rigidity; styrene also gives ABS its shiny surface.

note.simple: This is the only double bond, and it is used up when the molecule joins a chain. The rubber it makes has no C=C left for sunlight to attack.
note.deeper: The vinyl group polymerises to a saturated backbone, unlike butadiene, whose second double bond stays in the rubber.

note.simple: A side arm ending in a four-carbon tail.
note.deeper: n-Butyl acrylate is the usual monomer for the acrylate rubber in ASA.

name: PLA chain piece (4 L-lactic acid units)

groups.label: One repeat unit (from one lactic acid)

note.simple: One lactic acid, minus the water it lost when it joined on. A PLA chain is a very long row of these.
note.deeper: -O-CH(CH3)-C(=O)-, formula C3H4O2. Every stereocentre here is (S), as in poly(L-lactide).

note.simple: The link that holds each piece to the next. Water can slowly break it, faster when it is hot.
note.deeper: PLA is a polyester and degrades mainly by hydrolysis: water cuts the ester link and shortens the chain. Hydrolysis is also the first step when PLA breaks down in an industrial composter.

note.simple: A small bump on every unit. Because they all point the same way, the chains can fold into neat crystal patches.
note.deeper: In poly(L-lactide) every methyl sits on an (S) carbon; the regular stereochemistry is what lets PLA crystallise. Mixing in D units makes it more amorphous.

name: PETG chain piece (two PET units and one CHDM unit)

note.simple: Ethylene glycol plus terephthalic acid: the same unit drink bottles are made of.
note.deeper: -O-CH2-CH2-O-C(=O)-C6H4-C(=O)-, formula C10H8O4. In PETG some of these are swapped for the CHDM version.

note.simple: The extra ingredient that makes PET into PETG. Its big ring sticks out, so chains cannot pack into crystals.
note.deeper: 1,4-cyclohexanedimethanol replaces part of the ethylene glycol. It is six carbons bigger, disrupts crystallisation and leaves PETG a clear amorphous plastic.

note.simple: The link between the acid and the glycol. Water plus heat can cut it, which is why wet PETG strings and pops.
note.deeper: PET is hygroscopic: moisture in the melt hydrolyses ester links, shortening the chains.

note.simple: The stiff flat ring from terephthalic acid. It is what makes PETG rigid.
note.deeper: The para-phenylene ring in the backbone gives PET and PETG their stiffness and a glass transition well above room temperature.

name: TPU hard segment (MDI joined by butanediol)

note.simple: One MDI joined to one butanediol. A few of these in a row make a hard segment.
note.deeper: -C(=O)NH-C6H4-CH2-C6H4-NH-C(=O)-O-(CH2)4-O-, formula C19H20N2O4 (one MDI plus one butanediol, nothing lost when they join).

note.simple: The link that gives polyurethane its name. Its N-H on one chain grips the C=O on the next, so hard segments stick together.
note.deeper: A carbamate (-NH-C(=O)-O-). Hydrogen bonds between urethane groups pull the hard segments into ordered domains that act as physical cross-links.

note.simple: Stiff rings from MDI. They help the hard segments stack.
note.deeper: Aromatic hard segments pack well and melt high; Bambu measures the TPU 95A HF melt at 183 degrees C by DSC.

note.simple: Four carbons and an oxygen. Dozens of these make a long, floppy soft segment that coils up like a spring.
note.deeper: -O-(CH2)4-, from poly(tetramethylene ether) glycol (PTMEG), made from tetrahydrofuran. In MDI, butanediol and PTMEG elastomers the glass transition sits around -55 to -46 degrees C, so the soft segments stay rubbery in any weather.

note.simple: An oxygen holding two carbons. Bonds can swivel freely here, so the chain stays bendy.
note.deeper: Polyether soft segments resist hydrolysis much better than polyester ones, which is one reason some TPUs are polyether based.

name: ABS piece (a SAN branch grafted onto butadiene rubber)

note.simple: Styrene is the most common building block in ABS (about half of it). This is one styrene after joining the chain.
note.deeper: -CH2-CH(C6H5)-. ABS is a terpolymer, so there is no single repeat unit: typical grades are 40 to 60% styrene, 15 to 35% acrylonitrile and 5 to 30% butadiene.

groups.label: C=C double bond in the rubber

note.simple: Every butadiene unit keeps one double bond. Sunlight and oxygen attack here, the rubber goes hard and the part turns yellow and brittle.
note.deeper: Photo-oxidation of ABS starts in the polybutadiene phase: the C=C content drops and carbonyl groups form there before they appear in the SAN (Sabatini et al. 2023).

note.simple: Four carbons with a double bond in the middle. Long chains of these make the soft rubber blobs that stop ABS shattering.
note.deeper: A cis-1,4 polybutadiene unit, -CH2-CH=CH-CH2-. The SAN branch above grows off this rubber chain (grafting), which glues the rubber blobs into the glassy matrix.

note.simple: Nitriles on neighbouring chains pull on each other, making ABS stronger than plain polystyrene.
note.deeper: Polar C-N triple bonds; acrylonitrile adds chemical resistance, hardness and a higher heat deflection temperature.

note.simple: The bulky ring that makes the glassy part hard and shiny.
note.deeper: Phenyl side groups stiffen the SAN chains.

sources.label: Sabatini et al. 2023, Polymers 15:3267 (light-stability of ABS in LEGO bricks)

note.simple: Four carbons with one double bond left over from butadiene.
note.deeper: -CH2-CH=CH-CH2-, cis-1,4. The cis kink stops the chains packing, so the rubber stays soft and stretchy.

note.simple: The weak spot. Every unit has one, so there are lots of places for sunlight and oxygen to attack.
note.deeper: Unsaturated rubbers such as polybutadiene are among the most sensitive to ozone and photo-oxidation, because there is a C=C in every repeat unit.

name: ASA piece (a SAN branch grafted onto acrylate rubber)

note.simple: Styrene is the main building block of the glassy part of ASA, just as in ABS.
note.deeper: -CH2-CH(C6H5)-. The glassy matrix is the same styrene-acrylonitrile copolymer (SAN) as in ABS; only the rubber differs.

note.simple: The rubber in ASA is made of butyl acrylate. Its backbone has only single bonds, so sunlight has no C=C to snap.
note.deeper: Poly(n-butyl acrylate) rubber has no backbone double bonds, which gives ASA about ten times the weathering and UV resistance of ABS.

note.simple: One rubber building block: a single-bonded backbone piece with a floppy side arm.
note.deeper: -CH2-CH(COOC4H9)-. The SAN branch grows off a rubber chain like this one (grafting), anchoring the rubber blobs in the glassy matrix.

note.simple: Nitriles on neighbouring chains pull on each other and make the plastic tougher.
note.deeper: The same polar nitrile groups as in ABS.

note.simple: The bulky ring that makes the glassy part hard.
note.deeper: Phenyl side groups stiffen the SAN chains.

note.simple: One rubber building block. Notice the backbone: single bonds only.
note.deeper: -CH2-CH(COOC4H9)-, formula C7H12O2.

note.simple: The floppy side arm that keeps this rubber soft. There is no C=C anywhere for sunlight to break.
note.deeper: Acrylate rubber differs from butadiene rubber by the absence of double bonds.
